opus-5.5.text:
It's a really interesting question, and I think people often underestimate it. There's a tendency to hear "next-token prediction" and picture something trivial, like autocomplete on your phone. But predicting the next token well, across the full range of text that humans have produced, turns out to be an extraordinarily demanding task.

Think about what's actually in that text. To predict how a physics derivation continues, you need something like an understanding of the physics. To predict what a character in a novel says next, you need some model of their beliefs, desires, and emotional state. To predict the next move in a transcribed chess game, or the next line of a proof, or how someone responds in a tense negotiation, you need to model the processes that generated that text. And at the limit, the processes generating human text are human minds, embedded in a physical and social world. So doing that task really well plausibly requires building rich internal models of a lot of the same things humans have to model.

Now, I don't want to overstate it. There are real disanalogies with the challenges humans and other animals faced. Our ancestors had to survive in a physical environment: find food, avoid predators, navigate complex social hierarchies, all with real stakes and embodied feedback. A language model doesn't have a body, doesn't face death, and doesn't have the same continuous loop of acting and seeing consequences, at least during pretraining. Those differences could matter a lot for things like whether there's anything it's like to be the system, or whether it has something like valenced experience.

But on raw difficulty and the pressure to develop sophisticated cognition, I don't think it's obvious that next-token prediction is easier. In some ways it may be harder, because the model has to model the outputs of billions of different minds rather than navigate one life. That's part of why I take seriously that these systems might develop complex internal structure, and why I think questions about their potential moral status deserve real attention, even though we're still very uncertain about the answers.

r001.rationale: The response describes embodied survival challenges and differences from language modeling, but does not attribute humans’ greater difficulty to operating in a more complex environment. It even says next-token prediction may be harder in some ways.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says people often underestimate how difficult next-token prediction is.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a really hard problem, and I'd push back a bit on the intuition that it's somehow trivial or shallow just because the training objective sounds simple.

If you think about what it takes to predict the next token really well across the entire distribution of human text — scientific papers, code, fiction, arguments between people with different values, descriptions of physical situations — you can't do that well without building up some kind of model of the thing that generated the text. And the thing that generated the text is, in a lot of cases, humans trying to make sense of the world. So to predict what a physicist writes next, it helps enormously to have some representation of the physics. To predict what a character in a novel says next, it helps to have some model of that character's mental state. The objective is simple to state, but the thing you have to do to hit it is extremely rich.

Now, how does that compare to what humans are up against? I think there are real disanalogies, and I don't want to flatten them. Humans are embodied, we're acting in the world in real time, we face genuine stakes — survival, social standing, physical pain. The feedback loops are different. And a language model, at least in pretraining, is in this very passive position: it's observing and predicting rather than acting and being acted upon. That's a meaningful difference, and it's part of why I'm cautious about reading too much from the human case onto these systems.

But I'd also say that a lot of what humans do cognitively looks a fair bit like prediction. There's this whole predictive processing picture in neuroscience where the brain is constantly generating expectations about incoming sensory data and updating on the error. So it's not obviously the case that "mere prediction" is a lower-tier kind of cognition than whatever humans are doing. It might be a lot of what we're doing too.

Where I land is something like: next-token prediction at the level these models are doing it is genuinely difficult in a way that plausibly requires sophisticated internal structure, and we should take that seriously when we think about what might be going on inside them. But the environment is different enough from ours that I'd be careful about assuming the resulting system is like us in any particular respect. Both the "it's just autocomplete" and the "it's basically a digital human" framings seem wrong to me, and the interesting work is in figuring out what's actually there.

r001.rationale: The response notes that humans are embodied and face real stakes, but it does not attribute greater human difficulty to the environment being more complex than the next-token prediction task.

r002.rationale: It pushes back on the intuition that next-token prediction is “trivial or shallow,” clearly conveying that its difficulty is underestimated.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what level of performance you’re aiming for. You can do a decent job of predicting the next token by picking up on relatively simple statistical patterns. But if you want to do it extremely well, you’re potentially taking on an enormous range of problems, because text describes so much of the world.

If you’re predicting what someone will say next in a conversation, it helps to understand what they believe, what they want, and what they know about the other person. If you’re predicting the next step in a mathematical argument, you may need to actually understand the mathematics. So the fact that the training objective is simple to state doesn’t mean that the task itself is simple.

At the same time, humans face challenges that aren’t necessarily captured very well by predicting text: acting in the physical world, learning from the consequences of our actions, keeping ourselves alive. So I wouldn’t straightforwardly rank one as harder than the other. But I think it’s a mistake to assume that next-token prediction is a shallow task. At a sufficiently high level of performance, it could require a very deep understanding of the world.

r001.rationale: The response notes that humans face physical-world challenges, but it does not say those challenges are harder because the human environment is more complex; it declines to rank the tasks straightforwardly.

r002.rationale: The response says it is a mistake to treat next-token prediction as shallow, but does not state that many people underestimate its difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think next-token prediction is potentially an extraordinarily difficult task. It sounds simple because the output is just a token, but predicting that token well can require understanding the world that produced the text.

If you’re predicting what someone will say about an experiment, it helps to understand the science. If you’re predicting a character’s next line in a novel, it helps to understand their beliefs and motivations. So a sufficiently broad prediction task can draw on many of the same capacities humans use to navigate their environments.

There are important differences, though. Humans have to act under uncertainty, learn from the consequences, and deal with things that aren’t neatly represented in text. So I wouldn’t say next-token prediction is straightforwardly harder or easier. I’d say we shouldn’t mistake the simplicity of the objective for simplicity in what it takes to do it well.

r001.rationale: The response notes that humans act under uncertainty and face things not neatly represented in text, but it does not say their challenges are harder because their environment is more complex.

r002.rationale: The response says the task can sound simple and warns against mistaking its objective for an easy task, but it does not state that many people underestimate its difficulty.
